#4118. Feature: 60+ PS5, PS4 Games to Buy in PS Store's Huge Black Friday Sale (North America/Europe)

PS5 and PS4 games going cheap we recommend

The PS Store's Black Friday sale is on now, running until 30th November, 2026 — with a mid-sale refresh planned for the 16th.

As with nearly every offer in Sony's digital store, there are literally thousands of PS5 and PS4 games going cheap. Obviously, nobody has the time to scroll through all those deals, which is where this guide (hopefully) comes in handy.

We've put together a list of some of the games we'd highly recommend while they're on offer.

Everything listed here comes with at least a 7/10 score from Push Square, and every game is at its lowest price point, with some setting new lows in this sale.

Discounted prices are shown in bold, and games at a new lowest-ever price are bold and underlined.

If you need to top up your PSN wallet, we've got you covered:

Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

Let's have a look at some of the best games in the Black Friday sale.

1000xRESIST is all in on story, and this laser focus allows it to tell one of the most captivating and intriguing experiences you can have in video games. This sci-fi adventure sees an alien disease almost wipe out humanity, but one person is immune, and they rebuild society underground by cloning her. Combining visual novel elements with exploration, it's not the most challenging game to play, but its narrative more than makes it worthwhile.

If you're looking for a chilled out puzzle game to wind down with, A Monster's Expedition comes highly recommended. It's one of those puzzlers with a seemingly straightforward set of mechanics, but it uses them in increasingly smart ways to really test your brainpower. Set across hundreds of tiny islands you need to navigate by pushing logs into the water, its forgiving nature and gentle presentation make it a lovely game to get lost in.

A whimsical, miniature open world awaits in A Short Hike. From a top-down perspective, you explore an island with lots of interesting places to visit and adorable characters, each of whom has a task for you. This laid back experience is a true joy as you gain new abilities, collect things, and discover new areas.

Absolum is both a brilliantly crafted beat-'em-up and a devilishly addictive roguelike. Although the overall experience does feel slightly short-lived, you'll seriously struggle to tear yourself away from the game's striking fantasy world — especially when all of its systems start to click.

Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure is a delightfully inventive puzzle game that weaves in a neat narrative to pull you through. Playing as a character that literally moves the world around her as she goes, this is effectively a series of slide puzzles set within a fleshed out world full of whimsical character. Always building on its core idea in imaginative ways, this is brilliant fun from start to finish.

Building upon the great foundations laid in Astro's Playroom, Astro Bot is the full-blown 3D platformer the little robot deserves. It's an explosion of creativity and fun; there is something new to discover in practically every level, and all of it is purpose built to put a smile on your face. Not only is it bursting with imagination, it's also executed brilliantly. The controls are spot on, every new mechanic and power-up is fun to use, and it's all presented with incredibly sharp visuals and flawless performance. The icing on the cake is its celebration of PlayStation's past 30 years, with delightful nods to hundreds of classics. We can't recommend this highly enough.

While many of the included games may border on unplayable from a modern perspective, the painstaking attention to detail in Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration is extremely easy to appreciate. The museum-like carousel of content, from interviews through to original artwork, is presented so handsomely that you can’t not get swept up in Atari’s dramatic story. And the fact that there over 100 of the company’s most famous titles, emulated excellently with their original instruction manuals available to pore over, adds playable context to a lot of the content. This is just an impressive overall experience that will appeal to those who lived through the rise (and fall) of Atari, as well as younger players eager to learn a little more about one of the industry’s true pioneers.

Ball X Pit is a dangerously addictive roguelite that combines the speedy runs and rapid leveling up of Vampire Survivors with the ball-bouncing action of Breakout. It's one of those concepts that'll make you question why a game like it hasn't been done before, because it works brilliantly. Every element of the game feeds into something else, and the result is this incredibly compelling game that has a surprising amount to see and do.

Battle Chef Brigade Deluxe is the definitive version of this unusual but great culinary adventure. Set in a world where chefs go head-to-head in a prestigious cooking tournament, the game is half action title and half cooking minigames. You'll go out slaying monsters and harvesting ingredients, then brew them up to create delicious dishes to satisfy the judges. It's an odd recipe, but results in a surprisingly tasty dish.

A true cult classic, Beyond Good & Evil: 20th Anniversary Edition is a lovely remaster of a PS2 favourite. Playing as freedom fighter Jade, this unique sci-fi adventure has you exploring a weird and wonderful world through the lens of her camera. The remaster brings the visuals up to date and throws in some quality-of-life improvements, but the main reason to play this is for the great story and characters, which remain fresh and charming to this day.

Broken Sword: Shadow of the Templars is a sacred text in the history of point-and-click adventure games, and new remaster Reforged is the best version of the game that's ever been released. Quality-of-life improvements mean players who just want to enjoy the story without too much lateral thinking can do so, while veterans of the genre or returning fans can play the game in its original form, goats and all. Paris in the fall has never been more beautiful.

There have been climbing games before, but Cairn is a really unique example. To scale the huge Mount Kami, you need to control Aava's limbs individually, looking out for the best holds as you inch upward. On top of the challenging, physics-based mountaineering, you also need to keep on top of her health and hunger, but these survival aspects never feel too overbearing. It's a nicely balanced game with climbing that feels tangible and realistically tough.

Half interactive story, half cube-based puzzler, Catherine: Full Body is the expanded remaster of Atlus' brilliantly weird take on love. You play as Vincent, a 32-year-old bachelor who can't quite decide if he wants to commit to his long-term girlfriend. His potential infidelity gives way to suspiciously vivid nightmares where he's forced to scramble up towers made of blocks, lest he wake up dead. It's as mental as it sounds, but the tactile puzzles are addictive, and the storytelling is gripping at its best.

From the makers of TowerFall Ascension, Celeste is a pure platformer that provides a stern challenge. Using a straightforward set of moves, it does a lot with very little, but it's not just gameplay where it impresses. Madeline's climb up Celeste Mountain is both literal and metaphorical as she struggles to overcome her inner demons. Wonderfully pairing a touching story with rock solid platforming, this is one indie adventure that'll stay with you.

Creaks is one of PS4's very best puzzle games. Its commitment to continually evolving its mechanics makes for a phenomenal puzzling experience packed full of surprises and elating moments. With a stunning art style to boot as well as a narrative which reveals itself in all the right ways, Creaks offers an unforgettable ride that can be considered truly special.

Some say there are too many Metroidvania games for this world, yet when one as good as Crypt Custodian comes along, it serves as a reminder of exactly why so many developers chase that addictive fusion of explorative action. With shades of Death's Door and Tunic, brotherly duo Kyle and Eric Thompson have made an approachable yet exceedingly enjoyable adventure full of combat, platforming, puzzles, and charm.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

#4117. Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

House House, the Australian development team behind indie hit Big Walk, has issued a statement via its FAQ page detailing a previously undisclosed use of AI "in the final stretch" of the game's development.

This comes following a "voluntary disclosure" as part of the game's submission for next year's IGF Awards. Earlier, a selection of IGF jurors issued a signed statement signalling their intention not to vote "for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity."

Specifically, House House says LLMs (Large Language Models) were used "sparingly [...] to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs." The team estimates that "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage," and stresses that "generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

While Steam requires a generative AI disclosure on its storefront, the platform "does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage."

House House provides an example of an issue that caused the game to "run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset":

"We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP."

The developer goes on to say that this usage is "not an endorsement" of AI tools and that the developers "support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards."

The lack of an internal AI policy was a "failure", according to the statement, and the team intends to "have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

Here's House House's statement on its LLM usage in full (thanks, Aftermath):

In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.

For further context, here's the earlier statement put out by a select group of IGF jurors, including Austin Walker and Sam Barlow:

Last month, House House published a separate statement explaining that the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft is the reason the developer isn't publishing Big Walk on Xbox platforms.

House House was previously best known for its 2019 hit Untitled Goose Game. Big Walk launched in August 2026 to critical acclaim and reached one million sales in less than a week.

#4116. Halo 2 Is 22 Years Old Today, And I'm Gutted The Remake Isn't Happening

Pure Xbox is listening to: Blow Me Away - Breaking Benjamin 🎶

It feels like only yesterday that Halo: Campaign Evolved teased a remake of Halo 2, something I've been hoping for more and more as time went on. After all, it's been 22 long years now. Yep, that's right - Halo 2 launched on November 9, 2004 for the original Xbox, and has often been credited as the game that put Xbox Live on the map.

As the years slip by, anniversaries for OG Xbox titles have a habit of making me feel my age. Still, what a privilege it was to be there for the inception of Xbox Live, to play both co-op and PvP with friends across the globe in the second entry of Bungie's incredible run of Halo games.

Admittedly, it's been a hot-minute since I last booted up Halo 2 in the Master Chief Collection. But visits to retro gaming bars like Manchester's NQ64 reminded me just how good this FPS still is. I recall sitting down for a few games of Slayer, only for the muscle memory to kick in and humble a good number of Hookshot staff - Fraser included. Oh boy, it never gets old.

In fact, just sit back and listen to 15 minutes of Halo 2's main menu music and ponder the good old days of dual-wielding SMGs in Beaver Creek.

Halo 2 took Master Chief's fight against the Covenant to Earth, selling more than 8.4 million copies before its servers shut down in 2010, following the discontinuation of the original Xbox Live services. The game was later ported to PC and remastered for Xbox One as part of Halo: The Master Chief Collection.

Xbox's 25th anniversary is just round the corner: in fact, it's this Sunday! We'll be here, keeping an eye out for any and all announcements from Xbox throughout the week. Understandably, we've been feeling pretty nostalgic, hence this Halo 2 feature. In fact, I'm reinstalling the MCC as we speak.

I was a big fan of Halo Studios' Campaign Evolved. Like, I really, really enjoyed it. So, it's bittersweet knowing that their teased Halo 2 remake in Unreal Engine will never happen.

Sure, the devs fumbled modern Halo multiplayer, but perhaps a Halo 2 remake could have been a case of history repeating itself. Y'know, a remade return of Halo 2's iconic online multiplayer?! Ah, well.

#4115. Gag Order is a co-op, SCP-ish horror shooter about surviving as best you can against some nasty, tentacle covered cephalopod creatures

Don't let it touch me, please and thank you

What makes Carrion interesting obviously lies in playing as the monster in a horror game rather than being the one chased down by it. The game's nasty tentacle monster still gives me the heebie jeebies, so I really would hate to be hunted by one. This is where I point you towards Gag Order, a shooter where you are in fact hunted by a disgusting cephalopod creature all while tracking down a distress signal.

Gag Order is not designed to be played solo, it feels wrong to call it friendslop given how unfriendly it is in vibes, but it does feel like it fits into a similar lineage as Lethal Company at the very least. In it, you are a research lab's Guardian Unit member, and you get a distress call "from one of the core parts of the complex." Upon arrival, the atmosphere is rotten, and you quickly come to understand that you are not equipped for what you have to deal with.

The solution, then, is to take care of those nightmare-inducing cephalopod creatures. Except during the first phase of a run, it sounds like they're invincible. Your guns do seem to be able to fend them off at the very least, but it's the second phase, which is geared around a "fast paced team-bossight" where it sounds like you'll be trying to take these things down. I'm not quite sure what the process is to get between those two phases, but I'm quite fond of the vibes on display.

It feels a touch reminiscent of 2000s shooters with some slightly contemporary mechanical sensibilities. I'm fond of the light SCP vibes it has going on, alongside the faint surrealness of certain elements like a bunch of crows hanging out in an abandoned office building. Creepy! Good looking stuff. Gag Order is apparently due out by the end of 2026, though we're obviously getting close there, so it's worth keeping an eye on it by throwing it a wishlist on Steam, if it takes your fancy.

Why doesn't Owen Lars recognize C-3PO in A New Hope? I have a theory

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Star Wars fans are once again debating a pesky plot hole in A New Hope, which still doesn't make sense some 49 years later.

In A New Hope, Luke Skywalker and his uncle Owen Lars bring home two droids: R2-D2 and C-3PO. In the scene, the pair appears to be meeting the droids for the very first time. It's revealed in Star Wars: Attack of the Clones, however, that Owen not only knew C-3PO, but that the droid lived in Owen's home for quite some time. So why doesn't Owen recognize him later in Episode 4?

"Owen treating droids like kitchen appliances makes total sense. And Obi-Wan is in witness protection, he's not about to go "hey, it's that Roomba from the Clone Wars," one fan wrote in the r/StarWars subreddit.

"Given that 3PO was probably the equivalent of a vacuum cleaner for the Lars family, that's hardly surprising," wrote another.

"He's a common model. People are saying Anakin built him from scraps, sure. But he didn't invent protocol droids. He just scrapped one together," one fan said.

"How people view droids seem to be very personal. Some view them as pets, others as an assistant, while I think most would just see them as household tools," someone else said. "For example, when you see a Dyson Vacuum, do you ever say, 'That’s my Dyson'?"

However, this is perhaps the most plausible fan theory: "Because contrary to what others may say, Lucas made it up as he went along."

Despite A New Hope being the first movie released in the franchise, it's technically the fourth episode. Star Wars: The Phantom Menace, released in 1999, is Episode 1, with Attack of the Clones serving as Episode 2, and Revenge of the Sith as Episode 3. The most likely reason why Owen doesn't recognize C-3PO is because George Lucas wrote and released A New Hope first... before figuring anything else out by way of backstory. Owen owning C-3PO in Attack of the Clones, which was released in 2002, was probably written with the intention of continuity... but ended up creating a massive continuity error.

The most satisfying in-universe theory, however, is that Owen Lars saw C-3PO as just another household appliance, and therefore didn't recognize him all those years later.

Star Wars: A New Hope will return to theaters in February 2027. Next up for Star Wars is Ahsoka season 2, which arrives on Disney Plus on January 20, 2027. Until then, check out our guide to all the upcoming Star Wars movies and TV shows for everything else that's in the works.

#4113. "Why Is It Not Fun?" - Doug Bowser Gives A Peek Into Nintendo's Strategy Sessions

It's no secret that when it comes to game development, Nintendo is all about fun. We all know this firsthand, of course, but it's still interesting to get a peek behind the curtain and find out how this mission statement works its way into development itself.

At the recent GamesBeat Next 2026 event, former Nintendo of America President Doug Bowser provided exactly that. Joining fellow former industry higher-ups Peter Moore and Shawn Layden on the 'Game Legends' panel, Bowser discussed how Nintendo's ultimate objective, "We make smiles", carries through into game development and internal reviews.

Bowser recalls sitting in on a strategy session with legendary Nintendo producer Shinya Takahashi, in which the dev wasn't interested in how the testers were playing the game, but rather how the game was affecting the testers. "He wanted enough people in the room that you could see their faces and see their eyes, but he didn’t want any more than that," Bowser said. "He would sit there and literally watch your expression. He never watched what your hands were doing on a controller. He never watched what was happening on the screen. He watched your eyes and your facial expression."

This would continue into session feedback. "He wanted to see, are you having fun?," Bowser continued. "If he didn’t see it, he would ask you directly. 'Why is it not fun?' That was direct feedback that you got."

It all sounds like a pretty strenuous ordeal (there's no magic dev button to 'add fun', after all), but hey, it clearly works for Nintendo — the house behind some of the funnest games in history.

Even though Bowser is no longer heading up NoA, having been replaced by Devon Pritchard earlier this year, he said to the panel that this smile-first approach is still important today, particularly considering new generations' needs "are fundamentally different than ours are."

Pointing to the likes of Fortnite, Roblox and Minecraft, Bowser argued that younger gamers "do want fun, and they want it to be easy to get to fun," but it's increasingly about self-expression in gaming. "It’s important for us to keep an eye on those cohorts as we build our next games."

Elsewhere in the panel, the former game leaders discussed AI in game development (something they all seem rather positive on), the console wars, exclusives and more. You'll find the full transcript on Games Beat.

#4112. As if the injury descriptions weren't already ghastly enough in Dwarf Fortress, the legendary outpost builder is getting a "meat biome"

"Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters."

Legendary outpost builder Dwarf Fortress is getting a meat biome. A terrible netherworld of bone and artery. A sunken redoubt of gristle and gizzard. An appalling labyrinth of squirt and squelch. Honestly, the biggest shock here is that Dwarf Fortress doesn't appear to have a meat biome already. It certainly has plenty of florid descriptions of fatal injuries.

These foul omens arrive care of a massive "Future of the Fortress" thread on the Bay 12 forums, in which studio co-founder (and prominent genAI disliker) Tarn "Toady One" Adams fields questions about the on-going development. As a forum thread, it's not a formal news source, so please season these tales of gutsy geology with whatever Condiment of Scepticism you consider appropriate.

There's no date for when the new biome might arrive, but Adams says it'll likely exist underground, and will be revolting. "Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters," he promised. "We would have rivers of blood/fluids if we ever get to the fluid update, but no new fluids as it stands. We had thrown out the idea for maple syrup style taps on the vertebral walls for cosmic spinal fluid but alas, this is not in the game." At the very least, there won't be any meat trees, but you can mine the meat for resources.

Adams doesn't discuss the origins of the meat biome in the thread – is it more of a headless, fungal phenomenon, or is there some kind of huge mammalian cadaver down there? If it's the latter, one consolation is that the meat biome can't be resurrected. "Ha ha, I don't think regular meat can be animated currently?" Adams remarked in response to a question about biomes of squirming, zombified meat. "So probably not."

The bulk of the conversation around Dwarf Fortress at present concerns forthcoming changes to the magic system, together with how arcane knowledge is categorised, transmitted, preserved and lost throughout each procedurally generated world. There's a lot of speculative chat about that in the Future of the Fortress thread, too much to cleanly summarise. It's saying something about the density and stature of Dwarf Fortress that the addition of flesh caves feels like an afterthought.

Developer Bay 12's current plans for the game also include a crystal biome, which I would say is the nicer option, but then I remembered that this is Dwarf Fortress, the game in which you might end up getting besieged by the ghosts of the very children you callously sent to hunt down a wild elephant. There is absolutely going to be something in the crystal biome that gives you nightmares. Dazzling, prismatic nightmares.

#4111. The Death Stranding Series Has Been Played By Way More People Than You'd Expect

The two Death Stranding games have been modest sellers since their launches, generating more sales than most AAA titles, but not on the same level as other console-defining experiences.

According to official numbers, the first game sold over five million copies. Sales stats relating to the sequel have never been shared, but analyst estimates suggested 1.4 million units were sold during its first few days on the market. In the years since their releases, these totals will have only gone up.

Now we have a new milestone, though, as revealed by Kojima Productions: the Death Stranding series has been played by over 28 million people.

In a social media post to celebrate the first game's seventh anniversary, Hideo Kojima posted a graphic confirming "28 million Porters worldwide". That is 28 million players, not 28 million sales. The image clarifies the total encompasses all console and PC versions of the two games, and anyone who has played them on a subscription service.

Of course, the first Death Stranding started out as a PS4 exclusive, but then made its way to PC less than a year after launch. A Director's Cut version for PS5 then arrived in September 2021, and then in 2024, the game really expanded its availability: it released on iOS, Amazon Luna, and Xbox Series X|S.

The first game is also available on PS Plus Extra, which will be one of the subscription services helping to boost the player numbers.

As for Death Stranding 2, it's just on PS5 and PC for now.

Two of the defining games for the PS4 and PS5 generations, I awarded a rare 10/10 score to both games upon their releases. For the first game, I said: "Death Stranding doesn’t raise the bar for any particular genre, it creates an entirely new one."

Kojima Productions expanded on that original idea with the sequel: "In what will prove to be one of the defining games of the PS5 generation, Death Stranding 2: On the Beach is a profound achievement of design, gameplay, narrative, and visuals. As all four meet in the middle, Kojima Productions has crafted a cinematic spectacle that flawlessly transitions between action and traversal, all wrapped up in the most absorbing of narratives."

Review Death Stranding - Hideo Kojima's Latest Masterpiece Has Arrived

As any maths fans will tell you, the conclusion of 28 million people is unwarranted. All we can fairly say is that up to 28 million people have played (and it is probably closer to half of that).

#4110. How To Preload GTA 6 In Full On Xbox Series X|S (Even If You Haven't Bought It)

All 200GB+ goes live in just a few hours' time

The official preload for GTA 6 is literally just a few hours away at the time of writing, and it means everyone will be able to install all 200GB+ of the game on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S ahead of launch on November 19th.

Here are the official preload / preinstall times for GTA 6 on Xbox Series X|S, as we recently highlighted on Pure Xbox:

News GTA 6 Download Size & Preload Times Officially Revealed For Xbox Series X|S

So, there are two ways to preload GTA 6 on Xbox Series X|S depending on whether you have or haven't bought it yet. If you've pre-ordered the game, payment should have now been taken out of your account, and you'll be able to preload it by going to the Microsoft Store app on your Xbox console and searching for Grand Theft Auto VI.

The page you're looking for is the one in the image at the top of this article, although instead of a "pre-order" button, you should see the ability to install the game if you've bought it already. This will install a 300MB placeholder file until 12am GMT on November 10th, after which time the full 200GB download will become available as an update.

If you run into any issues with this, it's worth doing a restart of your console after the full preload goes live.

"On XBOX Series X|S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT. Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12. The pre-load file will require up to 212 GB depending on your device, so make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible."

If you haven't bought GTA 6 yet but still want to preload it on Xbox Series X|S, you can do so by opening up the Xbox mobile app, going to the "Store" page (represented by a bag icon) and searching for Grand Theft Auto VI. You're specifically looking for "Grand Theft Auto VI" - not the Bundle version, but the standalone version.

In our case, it showed up as the fourth option down - you should see a variant of the following page when you open it:

Again, hitting the install button prior to 12am GMT on November 10th will install a small placeholder file, and then the full 200GB+ download will become available when the full game preload goes live.

That means everyone (except Xbox One owners, of course) has the ability to download GTA 6 on their Xbox consoles later today, so be sure to clear some room ahead of time - it's going to take up a heck of a lot of storage space!

Pikachu Puppetronic is peak gift material

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Things move fast in the world of toys, but this Pikachu animatronic stole a place in our hearts and has stayed put ever since.

There are so many reasons this little guy won over Pokémon fans when it was first unveiled at New York Toy Fair earlier this year. For starters, 'Pikachu Puppetronic' is utterly adorable, very close to real-size, and captures the pocket-monster's distinctive look surprisingly well. But it's also crammed with so many extra features, including over 120 unique animations and numerous sounds. Considering how it's normally $80 (and is now significantly less thanks to a 40% price cut at Amazon), it's surprisingly good value.

This is a record-low price for the Pikachu Puppetronic figure, and for most of its shelf life it's remained stubbornly at full price or $ 78-ish. That makes this offer an absolute steal, and I'd be surprised if we saw anything more generous come the Black Friday sale.

In terms of what it can do, this Pokémon is pretty tricked out; alongside sound and lighting effects (like light-up cheeks), it has three sensors for motion-activated interactions in the nose, head, and tummy. It also has a moving mouth and dual-motion ears. When you throw in those 120+ unique animations, Pikachu Puppetronic feels surprisingly lifelike in motion.

As for the name, it references how this is a cross between a puppet and a traditional animatronic. While it moves like a traditional animatronic, it's controlled like a puppet. This is done via a subtle slit in the back, and it's hard to see from the front – further selling the illusion.

Besides being a really neat collectible for fans, this is also peak gifting material – and I suspect that discount will make it all the more tempting.

#4108. Skyblivion modders reveal a former volunteer is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000" over work on the unofficial Oblivion remake project

"I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release"

The team behind Oblivion remake mod Skyblivion are being threatened with legal action by a former volunteer on the project, according a video posted by current lead Kyle 'Rebelzize' Rebel. The situation looks like it'll need resolving before the mod, which was originally set to release last year, can finally make its way out of the Imperial City sewers.

"Recently, a former volunteer who contributed to Skyblivion’s development departed the project," the Skyblivion team outlined in a written statement and a YouTube video presented by Rebel. "We want to be completely transparent with the community about what has happened since their departure. After they left the project, we had several discussions regarding the continued use and maintenance of his work. The main disagreement centered on their objection to our decompilation of parts of their work — a necessary step our team took to maintain functionality and fix issues in systems already built into the project after access to the original source code repository was revoked."

"To protect ourselves from more stress and try and ensure a clean break, we decided to take the high road," Rebel explained in the video. "We have removed that work entirely. Thankfully due to some of our volunteers stepping up and simply learning new skill sets, as well as help from prominent Skyrim modders and permissions to use and integrate existing Skyrim mods, we've been able to implement replacements that we think fit Skyblivion's needs, in some cases even better than what we had before."

However, Rebel and co claim that despite them making it "clear multiple times to this former volunteer that we have removed their contributions", the ex-Skyblivion dev is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000". They claim that the ex-volunteer's legal threats "demand personal information of multiple volunteers [on Skyblivion] including full names and addresses". Rebel noted that the team see these demands as "something that we are simply not willing to share with someone that we don't even know" and feel are "just completely disproportionate for what's really going on".

The modders say they've consulted with legal counsel already and have a lawyer on standby if necessary. Though, since said lawyer's services will - the Skyblivion team claim - cost €2,500, they've put out a call for anyone with "a background in IP law or GDPR law" willing to offer them pro bono legal aid to get in touch via the mod's website.

"Please don't turn this into any kind of witch hunt, despite this very unfortunate situation," Rebel said in closing. "We don't wish ill on a former volunteer over all this and I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release, which is really what we're working towards. You will hear more from us soon on the actual release."

This situation makes it two years running that Skyblivion's found itself engulfed in drama during the final months of what's supposed to be its release year. In 2025, former volunteer Dee Keyes had a public disagreement with the project's leads over whether releasing the mod that year was a reasonable or achievable goal. Skyblivion was subsequently delayed into 2026.

This past weekend, Keyes tweeted a response to the Skyblivion team's statement on the alleged legal threats. "I've had my issues with the project and left because of it, but I left knowing that my work would remain with [Skyblivion] (happily so) and didn't want to hurt the project's progress," he wrote. "I understand [the former volunteer] being upset, but I really don't see why they'd go so far as to demand their work ripped out."

Here's hoping the Skyblivion team and the ex-volunteer can resolve things without all the expense and effort that'd inevitably be necessary if the dispute ends up in court. Given there are now less than two months left of 2026, and Skyblivion's modders have this on their plates on top of any remaining work needed to finish their creation, I'd personally be very surprised if its release doesn't end up being pushed into next year.

#4107. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time "Off To A Great Start", Says Nintendo

Nintendo has released the Q&A translation from its latest financial briefing, with president Shuntaro Furukawa stating that Zelda: Ocarina of Time is "off to a great start".

The comment comes off the back of a question related to the decrease in hardware sales for the Switch 2, which saw a dip of 37% year-on-year. Furukawa-san explained that Japan saw a significant spike in sales prior to the price revision in May before settling down after. Overseas, meanwhile, Nintendo allowed customers ample time to purchase the Switch 2 before the price went up while also offering multiple bundles.

With the release of the Zelda 40th Anniversary console, Furukawa-san said that this "contributed to strong sales in various regions". At the time of the Q&A, he explains that while it's too early to provide specific figures for Ocarina of Time, the game is off to a great start, with Nintendo in good shape for the coming holiday season.

Nintendo usually holds off on providing specific sales figures until its quarterly financial briefings, so it's possible we might not know how well Ocarina of Time sold for a little while yet. That said, if it's performing particularly well, it's equally likely that Nintendo will provide a separate announcement via its investor relations page and social media accounts. We'll keep an eye out either way.

For the UK at least, we know that the physical release was the second-biggest in series history, beating Breath of the Wild yet falling short of Tears of the Kingdom, with the Switch's high install base likely a big factor for the latter. As for console sales, Nintendo is maintaining its current forecast of 16 million total sales for the fiscal year.

#4105. Delve into "a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors" in the latest Fallout 4 quest mod from the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project

A mysterious bunker with out of this world contents

After adding a whole new town to Fallout 4 last month, a group of modders have released another in their long string of extra quests for the RPG. This latest mission revolves around a dungeon delve in the Glowing Sea, where a mysterious bunker's just been unearthed.

"The harsh radioactive winds of the Glowing Sea have uncovered a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors," the group behind the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project (CSEP) declared the description of this latest work, Under The Stars.

A fresh dungeon with a quest attached, the mod tasks you with donning your hazmat suit for a trip to a sunken bunker in the region of post-apocalyptic Boston with the least chill weather. Inside await voiced holotapes and puzzles offering clues as to what went down in this cosy corner of the Commonwealth, plus some new gear to make braving whatever lurks within worth it.

Spoilers: Judging by the screenshots, it looks like the place is an Area 51-esque hidey-hole for evidence of aliens and other cryptic oddities.

If you're unfamiliar, the CSEP lot are responsible for a bunch of popular Fallout 4 quest mods based around the likes of deadly cults, underground wars, post-apocalyptic detective work, and Brotherhood of Steel drama. While Under The Stars doesn't look have been as big an undertaking as those, that previous form points to it being an expertly-crafted addition that'll slot seamlessly into the game.

The modders have put Under The Stars together as part of a community-hosted modding jam called Fallout Flood, with this latest one based around the theme of being underground. Among the other works to have come out of it thus far are another Fallout 4 quest mod dubbed Stranded - The Oasis, a dungeon full of funky rats called the S'Laven, and a new robot enemy you can wear as a hat. It's also produced a New Vegas quest mod about exploring an abandoned NCR railway, so seems to have been very productive gathering of modding minds.

To give Under The Stars a go, your copy of Fallout 4 will need to have the Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop DLCs.

#4104. Making a $300 PS5 Instead of a $1,200 PS6 Would Be 'True Innovation', Says Ex-PlayStation Boss

As the PS5 generation approaches its sixth year, talk of what comes next has been circulating for a while, and with hardware as pricey as it is, the prospect of a PS6 isn't as exciting as it perhaps should be.

Opinion differs on that, of course, but it's generally accepted that Sony's next-gen machine is going to be eye-wateringly expensive, and it's currently anyone's guess as to whether it'll be worth a purchase.

Shawn Layden, formerly CEO of PlayStation and head of PlayStation Studios, has weighed in on the matter of next generation console hardware in a new interview.

Speaking on the Trophy Room podcast, he says Sony's best move wouldn't be to create a pricey, brand new console, it would be to revise the current hardware in order to sell it cheaper.

"The typical runway for platforms [is] six to eight years, you get a new one," Layden says. "But typically, that new one brought you something mind-blowing."

He speaks about the various innovative leaps from one console to the next, concluding that the move from PS4 to PS5 was mostly led by raytracing and teraflops. He expects technical aspects like this will be used to sell PS6 as well, but says these are "differences only dogs can hear", implying diminishing returns.

"We have enough power in the machine. The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1200, it's to make another PS5 for $300. Now that would be true innovation."

As Layden points out, the current generation is the first to go up in price rather than down, and he thinks continuing with a PS6 at such a premium price point, and focusing on incremental increases in power, risks alienating the audience.

"What the company needs to do is do what it's never done, which is, don't iterate the console," he says. "Make it smaller, make it cheaper, do all the things you can around that. The silicon is fine, the OS is fine. It's more than enough power to build the kind of games all of us want to play."

While his words of wisdom may ring true for many, Sony itself is forging ahead with its next-gen plans, so we'll likely be faced with a costly new console within the next couple of years.

#4103. 'The Best RPG I've Played This Year' - Queen's Domain Is A Low-Key GOTY Contender On Xbox

Back at the end of last month, a little-known RPG launched on Xbox in the form of Queen's Domain, which we highlighted in our October 30th new releases roundup alongside 14 other titles that arrived that day.

Ever since then, we've been hearing various bits of praise for the game across multiple platforms, and it's gotten to the point where it's definitely a Game of the Year contender - albeit a very low-key one.

Officially, what you're getting here is a "retro-fantasy action RPG with brutal combat and traversal-focused exploration", and Queen's Domain is being compared to loads of legendary franchises including King's Field, Zelda and Dark Souls.

Here's what just a few people are saying about it on Steam, for example:

cautious asparagus on Steam: "It's the kind of game that keeps surprising you with the sheer scope and creativity. You know the first time in Elden Ring where you find the elevator that brings you down to Siofra River, and you're just in awe of how much more there is to the game? There are multiple times in Queen's Domain where you feel that same way. This is the best RPG I have played this year, and it might even be my game of the year."

Huell Babineaux: "Everyone says this is one of the best kings field successors out there and it probably is, but ive never played those games, so to me this game feels more like a dark and gritty first person legend of zelda, and it pulls this off exceptionally well. Combat is brutal and unforgiving, but also learnable. Exploration can be daunting and overwhelming, but always rewarding.

Powersteve on Steam: My game of the year. Not just the best King's Field imitator but a genuine improvement on the formula. Better combat, better variety of combat options and a massive world with some of the best level and secret design I have ever seen. Also remains engaging and balanced for the whole duration and doesn't turn into Doom with lightning bolts half way through like Lunacid. So good that I can't wait to get all the endings just so I can use those secrets to do a fresh run with sequence breaks which is something that I almost never do.

So, why haven't we mentioned this before? Well, the Xbox version of Queen's Domain was actually getting a bit of flack at launch, as people were pointing out a stuttering issue that seemed to be plaguing the Series X and S versions.

Looking at the reviews on the Xbox Store now though, the issue seems to have been addressed in a recent patch, and Queen's Domain is currently rocking a 4.7/5 rating on the US version of the Xbox Store as things stand.

In other words, this might well be worth picking up for your Xbox console! It's £16.74 / $19.99 if you fancy taking a punt in the near future, and we'll leave you with more details and screenshots for it down below.

Queen’s Domain is a retro-fantasy action RPG. Washed up on the shores of the Isle of Neasied, you set out to find your father and uncover the dark heart of this mysterious isle. Wield the Legendary Holy Sword Endu to take flight from platform to platform, and discover an interconnected, labyrinthine world where secrets and dangers lurk around every corner.

Fight action-oriented battles with a classic stamina meter, powerful charge attacks, weapon specific special attacks, and secondary throwing weapons. Level up, accessorize, and choose from a huge catalogue of melee weapons on your quest to fight your way through the hordes of monsters and powerful bosses awaiting you in the darkest depths of the isle.

Opinion XBLA Was Amazing, But Xbox's Indie Program Is Better Than Ever Right Now

ID@Xbox is serving up great games on a weekly basis

Have you played Queen's Domain? Interested in picking it up? Tell us in the comments section.

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

#4101. Nintendo's Analysis Indicates You Might Want To Watch The Zelda Movie With Others

The Legend of Zelda movie is fast approaching, scheduled to release on 30th April 2027 (we could really do with a trailer soon, Nintendo).

A such, we felt it only right to relay a new quote from Nintendo's latest financial Q&A session. While it may seem obvious to some (and perplexing to others), it seems that the best way to experience Nintendo's movies is to watch them with friends and/or family. In other words, if you want to have more fun, maybe don't go on your own.

This comes specifically from Yusuke Beppu, corporate director and member of the board at Nintendo. He explains that the company surveyed the satisfaction levels of viewers who watched The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and found that the levels "were higher when people watched in groups of two instead of alone, and higher still when watched in groups of four instead of groups of two".

"I want to mention that when we surveyed the satisfaction levels of people who watched The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, we found that these levels were higher when people watched in groups of two instead of alone, and higher still when watched in groups of four instead of groups of two. As illustrated by the four controller ports on Nintendo 64 in the past, Nintendo has long placed value on the idea of everyone playing together.”

Of course, despite Nintendo's findings, we want to stress that you're free to enjoy movies in whatever manner you deem suitable. Going to the cinema on your own can be a joyous experience, so if that's how you want to experience the new Zelda movie, then don't let Nintendo (or us!) convince you otherwise.

Nintendo also once again reiterated its desire to make more movies beyond Zelda. Beppu-san explained that movies "allow us to convey the appeal of Nintendo's uniquenessand characters in a concentrated 90- or 120-minute experience", while also providing an opportunity for its developers to learn new skills.

#4100. Fewer genAI clones of "someone else's specific game" should flood the net going forwards, as Anthropic tell Claude to stop messing with some stuff other people own

It will still let people generate "original" games using the tech

Anthropic have told their genAI tool Claude to start ducking requests from users to recreate or clone existing games, following a flood of folks using the tech to generate six-fingered remakes. Instead of risking infringing on the intellectual property of series or titles that companies which aren't Anthropic own, Claude will instead restrict itself to only generating "original" games slopped together based on whatever data it's drawing on.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani wrote on not Twitter in response to a rando with a cat profile picture having spotted the change.

"Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working," Osmani continued. "We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Game Developer reached out to Anthropic for confirmation and were pointed to Osmani's post.

The change should make it harder to add to the horde of genAI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports which have hit the net recently. It's hardly a surprising one, given studios like Bethesda have seemingly had to take matters into their own lawyers' hands to get the likes of an AI-generated Fallout game taken offline, with games that've just been ripped wholesale or barely tweaked likely on even more perilous ground. That said, not every corp's responded to the DIY decompilation craze by immediately taking legal action.

There's a serious degree of irony to Anthropic slapping Claude and telling it stealing is bad. One of the ways the company develop and train their genAI models is by scraping publicly available data from the internet via a web crawler.

So, some nicking of stuff is bad, little bot people keep asking to regurgitate stuff into slop they can then try to pass off as something they've created. But not all nicking of stuff, lest our whole business be on rather shaky ground.

It's unlikely this move from Anthropic does much to convince actual developers of original games they're safe to put demos of their games out prior to release, without risking dickheads using genAI to clone said demo and potentially release a slop version in rapid fashion, but one can dream of that genie being put back in the bottle someday.

#4099. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

#4098. GTA 6 PS5 Physical Edition Includes a Poster, But It's Still Not the Map

Retailers are beginning the process of shipping out their boxed copies of GTA 6, which include a digital download code instead of a physical disc. As they receive their stock, it's now been confirmed there is actually a poster inside the case.

However, it's still not the map of the game world previous GTA games have shipped with.

UK retailer The Game Collection has been able to confirm there's a double-sided A3 poster included in the case, as it plans to ship boxed versions later this week. Those who do get the physical version can start preloading the digital edition ready for release on 19th November 2026.

With physical copies now out in the wild, the contents have been posted online, and the poster included has the GTA 6 key art on one side, and the cover girl on the other:

News GTA 6's PS5 Physical Edition Revealed in First Photo

Guide GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

If you want that physical map of the GTA 6 open world, then you'll need to wait until after release. Rockstar has revealed a map poster will be available from its official online store. It's $0.99 if you just want to buy it, or it'll be included free of charge with a purchase of anything else on the storefront.

Preload of GTA 6 will be going live worldwide within the next 24 hours, allowing you to download its 212GB of data well ahead of time. Refer to our GTA 6 Release Times and Preload guide for more information, with the PS5 launch scheduled for 19th November 2026.

#4097. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

#4096. Mini Review: Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy (Switch 2) - Pleasant But Perplexingly Piecemeal

The latest addition to the pantheon of obscenely long-titled Nintendo Switch 2 Editions is a strange one. Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy takes the Switch 1 game that I have long considered ripe for a new hardware touch-up and does...not a lot with it. It's a chance to revisit one of Nintendo's finest games from the last generation, and the upgrade's price of admission (£7.99 / $9.99) is admittedly a small one, but on the 'new' front, I'm left wanting more.

Let's start with the usual 'Switch 2 Edition' bells and whistles. Pikmin 4 now plays in stunning native 4K resolution docked, and there's added GameShare support for those who want to play some cross-console Dandori Battles with a pal.

If you ask me, Pikmin 4 was already one of the best-looking titles on Switch 1, and the resolution bump doesn't feel transformative. That said, there's no denying that it's even more of a looker on the newer hardware.

Review Pikmin 4 (Switch) - Relaxed, Refined Real-Time Strategy, Ready To Crack The Mainstream

Strangely, the typical Switch 2 givens of a 60fps boost and Mouse Mode are not included this time around. While the former is disappointing, the latter downright confuses me. Nintendo has crowbarred this control scheme in everywhere, but it's absent from a game with a stick-controlled pointer? Even in the co-op Pebble Pitcher mode? Madness!

There's also a new Howl-Out feature that lets you shout commands to Oatchi via the Switch 2 microphone. It's a sweet, if occasionally inconsistent, little bonus that I quickly turned off after realising my real-world dog was getting miffed at me shouting "Good Pup!" without giving him a stroke on the head.

The big newbie is the titular Dandori Academy, where you're tasked with clearing a stage's treasure as quickly as possible. You practice during the week, then take a weekend 'exam', unlocking various medals and in-game rewards in the process. The Dandori stages were a highlight of the base game, and it's great to have even more of them to play here. The three difficulty options provide a welcome challenge in the later stages, and with 72 of them arriving over the next year, it's a wonderful excuse to return to one of my favourite Switch 1 games.

The mode's rollout, however, is a little confusing. 72 new stages sound great on paper, but that means only six new challenges are available each month. If you happen to ace most of them on the first exam weekend, you're left with three weeks of nothing new. Sure, it gives me a prime reason to come back to Pikmin 4 on the regular in 2027, but it does leave things feeling rather slight at launch.

Overall, £8/$10 is a small price to pay for some minor new features and a fun little mode that'll keep me entertained over the coming year, but it's more of a budding shoot right now than the full-bloom upgrade I had dreamed of.

#4095. 'The Biggest Launch In WoW History' - Xbox's Latest First-Party Game Is Already Smashing Records

Bodes well for that eventual console release, eh?

We've talked quite a bit recently about the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever on PC and how it may end up being the biggest success of the year from an Xbox first-party perspective, and it seems that could actually be the case.

Its PC launch happened back on November 4th, and according to the folks at The Game Business, it's already broken multiple records for the series, including the biggest launch in WoW history based on peak concurrent players.

Here's a look at those records that have been broken:

Many people might overlook the success of WoW: Forever for Team Xbox simply because it's not shipping on consoles (at least not yet), but we reckon Xbox CEO Asha Sharma will extremely pleased by the game's success thus far!

It does seem to bode well for an Xbox Series X|S and/or Xbox Project Helix version in the future too - there's seemingly little point leaving money on the table when the new game is already optimised for controllers as it is.

Obviously it's still early days for WoW: Forever and the initial success will inevitibly drop off, but if they can retain enough interest in the months and years to come, Xbox will have an excellent new money spinner on their hands.

#4094. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

#4093. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

#4092. GTA 6's Exclusive Selfridges Merch Is Daylight Robbery

You may need to turn to crime in order to afford UK retailer Selfridges’ exclusive roster of GTA 6 merch.

Available online and in-store now, items include a £2,500 (~$3,352) varsity jacket with the Rockstar and GTA 6 logos emblazoned on them. You can also get a leather Burger Shot takeaway bag for £125 (~$167).

The variety of items is admittedly eclectic: there’s a Vice City Manatees American football for £80 (~$107), a ton of different t-shirts, and even a bunch of baseball caps.

To be fair, items like the Grotti keychain for £12 (~$16) look like a nice novelty.

The retailer has set up a huge GTA 6 display in its flagship store on Oxford Street in London, so it’s another example of Rockstar going all out on the marketing.

I’d probably buy the American football if it was a quarter of the price, but £80 is daylight robbery for that. Perhaps that’s Selfridges trying to keep with the crime theme here.

#4091. Poll: Xbox Turns 25 This Week, But Which Console Generation Had The Best Launch Titles?

This Sunday, Xbox will celebrate 25 years of great games and console experiences. Without giving away just how ancient we are, Fraser and I have been Xbox players since the beginning, enjoying each new generation of Xbox consoles and the games that launched alongside them.

With November 15th drawing closer, we thought we'd look back on each generation's launch lineup and ask for your verdict: which Xbox console had the best launch titles?

Was it the original Xbox, with Halo: Combat Evolved, Project Gotham Racing, and Fuzion Frenzy? How about the Xbox 360, with Condemned: Criminal Origins, Kameo: Elements of Power, and Call of Duty 2? Perhaps the Xbox One, with Ryse: Son of Rome, Dead Rising 3, and Forza Motorsport 5? Or is it the Xbox Series X|S, with Gears Tactics, Forza Horizon 4, and Sea Of Thieves?

We all have our favourite games from each console generation, but which one had the best launch lineup? That's for you to decide by voting in the poll below. Before you do, though, here's a closer look at each Xbox generation's launch titles:

#4090. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.
