James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios and will be replaced by former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

James Gunn and DC Studios co-CEO Peter Safran are stepping down as the heads of DC Studios and will be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham.

Per The Hollywood Reporter, Gunn and Safran are out of the job from December 1, 2026. That's just over four years after the pair were appointed to the post. In that time, DC Studios has released three movies (Superman, Supergirl and Clayface) and four TV shows (Creature Commandos, Peacemaker season 2, The Penguin and Lanterns). Projects currently in the pipeline include Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, Jimmy Olsen series The People v. Gorilla Grodd, Creature Commandos season 2, and Elseworlds movie The Batman: Part II.

“Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision," Gunn and Safran said in a statement. "In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. "We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with.

"We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter," Gunn and Safran said of their replacement at DC Studios. "We're excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow."

In a separate, longer statement on Threads, Gunn said he's "incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking" and noted "the characters we set up will live on".

Latcham is Marvel Studios' former senior VP of production and development, and was Kevin Feige's right-hand man at the company for a time, with credits on Iron Man, The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy and Spider-Man: Homecoming. As with Gunn and Safran, Latcham will oversee DC's film, TV and animation slate.

"James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of," Skydance bosses David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz said in a statement. "We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

What the future now holds for DC is now less clear than ever. While several projects from the Gunn and Safran era are still in the pipeline, many were critical of Gunn and Safran's decision not to launch their shared universe with big-hitters like Batman and Wonder Woman, and instead focus on lesser-explored characters like Supergirl and Clayface. Could a creative reboot be on the cards, despite Gunn's Superman movies still being an ongoing concern? We'll soon find out.

Man of Tomorrow releases on July 9, 2027. For more, here's all the upcoming DC movies and shows announced before Gunn's departure.

In a previous life as a print dinosaur, I was the Deputy Editor of Total Film magazine, and the news editor at SFX magazine. Fun fact: two of my favourite films released on the same day - Blade Runner and The Thing.

#4020. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

#4019. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

In a Thursday, November 5 interview with Yahoo Finance (via TechRadar), AMD CEO Lisa Su emphasized the company's AI commitments. Separately, in a Q3 2026 earnings call, Su forecasted an overall "dobule-digit" slump in PC sales in 2027.

"We're a tech company that has a lot of resources and the ability to expand our supply and expand our ability to help our customers. And that's what's led to tremendous growth. So being able to say that my data center business is going to grow 50% sequentially from Q3 to Q4, it's a big step up and it's a testament to how important computing is in the industry today.

"We're looking to double the business⁠—more than double the business⁠—as we go into next year. We are a data center-first company, that is our profile and people need more computing to power all these applications.

[Responding to a question about this past week's slump in AI and tech valuations] "I think the market can sometimes be a little bit short-sighted. Look, it is what it is. What I look at is in the long term, if you believe⁠—which I do, deeply⁠—that computing in many ways equates to intelligence. So the more compute you have, the more intelligent you are, the more intelligent your company is, the more problems you're going to be able to solve, the more you're going to accelerate your business.

"If you believe that foundation, then investing ahead of the curve is the right thing to do because we're always investing for the long term. Long term being, you know, three, four, five years and beyond. And that means you have to make the investments now.

"I've always operated AMD that way. We're always looking at, what do we see over the horizon? And over the horizon, I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives and every aspect of our business. So I believe in this demand and I very much believe that many of the investments that are being made throughout the ecosystem are also seeing some of these same trends."

I found Dr. Su's statements incredibly frustrating, and that all comes down to fundamental differences in perspective and incentive. I do not believe that "computing equates to intelligence" when the output of AI models is so unreliable. They have not changed my life or my work, except to make computer components prohibitively expensive. I do not see "super intelligence" becoming more essential to every aspect of my life in the coming years.

Dr. Su sees the post-US midterm election decline in tech stocks as Mr. Market being short-sighted, but I see overinvestment in data center buildouts and the ludicrous valuation of AI companies as the fundamental error. PC sales will undoubtedly slump next year as the RAMpocalypse continues, but it's hard to swallow tech leaders' sober prognostications on the subject when they caused the shortages and price increases driving the slump.

I believe⁠—and what's more, I hope⁠—that the fever will break and that there will be a correction. Unfortunately, with how much of the economy⁠—particularly 401ks and pension funds⁠—that has been bet on AI's continued growth, I think the coming hangover will be far more democratically distributed than the decision to go on the bender in the first place.

#4017. Guide: Cyberpunk 2077: Best Mods on PS5

What are the best Cyberpunk 2077 mods on PS5? In this guide, I'm going to highlight which mods I think are well worth installing to make your dark future experience more enticing.

On this page: Cyberpunk 2077: Best Mods on PS5

Mod support for Cyberpunk 2077 was added with Patch 2.5 on PS5, allowing for user-created content on Sony's console.

Choosing and installing mods is easy: just click the 'Mods' option on the game's main menu and you'll be taken to the current list of available mods. You can scroll through pages manually or you can use the search bar.

If you find a mod you like, select it from the list and then click the 'Install' button, or just press the Options button on your controller to install it right there and then.

You can also hit the 'Like' button to add the mod to your 'Liked' list. Doing this lets you keep track of your favourite mods via the 'Liked' filter button new the top of the screen.

You can have a maximum of 150 mods installed at any one time, and said mods need to have a combined file size of 15.76GB or under (although this isn't really an issue as of yet, as standard mod sizes tend to be very, very small).

Unfortunately, yes, using any mods disables Trophies when playing Cyberpunk 2077 on PS5.

This counts for any save file that has ever been used in conjunction with mods.

As such, you may want to beat the game at least once, or go all the way and get the Platinum, before diving into the world of mods.

Below, you'll find a list of what I think are currently the best Cyberpunk 2077 mods available on PS5.

Admittedly, the selection is far from vast at this point in time — but new mods are being added on what seems to be a weekly basis, and so this list should only grow over the coming months.

A mod that's bound to be at or near the top of Cyberpunk 2077's modding menu for years to come, Deceptious Quest Core is a necessary framework mod for a number of Deceptious' other mods.

Basically, you need to have this mod installed if you want a few of the other mods featured on this list — it's just the way that the game's quest-based modding works.

Any mod that has [DQC] in its title requires Quest Core to function.

Note that you need to enter V's H10 apartment (and then possibly exit it) for this mod to activate, and subsequently activate all of the [DQC] mods.

This mod aims to fix a surprisingly long list of bugs that are still found throughout Cyberpunk 2077.

The vast majority of these bugs are minor and only affect very small aspects of the overall game. We're talking things like slight animation glitches, specific audio mixing (those annoyingly quiet, and sometimes annoyingly loud TVs), and quest-related oddities.

Still, it's a mod worth installing when you start adding all of these fixes up — especially if you plan on starting a new playthrough.

This mod allows Johnny to appear in all of V's apartments, not just their starting home in the H10 megabuilding.

If you enjoy Johnny's company, this mod's good for immersion purposes. He'll lounge around the apartments, and add to the ambience by playing his guitar when V asks him to.

One of my favourite mods on PS5 so far, Weather Probability Rebalance does exactly what its name suggests, adjusting the chances of different weather patterns appearing as you carve out a life in Night City (and its surrounding wastelands).

For those who have already spent tens or even hundreds of hours playing Cyberpunk 2077, you may have noticed that the weather can be a bit... boring. The whole atmosphere of the city can change when it's raining, or when there's a sandstorm — but it can feel like it just doesn't happen often enough.

According to modder RMK_, the game's weather system is actually a little funky. In short, sunny weather can become 'stuck' under certain circumstances, and so this mod attempts to fix the problem.

As a result, adverse weather is much more common and lasts longer, allowing you to soak up the vibes.

A great mod for immersion purposes, Night City Interactions lets you go out drinking at various locations across the map — but the best part is that you can invite other characters, like Panam, Judy, River, and Kerry, to come along with you.

As a bonus, this mod also includes a Cyberpunk Edgerunners tour quest. As you may know, the anime features a number of backdrops that are based on actual locations from the game, and you can check these specific places out at your leisure.

Note that you need to enter V's H10 apartment (and then possibly exit) before this mod activates.

Three small mods that add just an extra touch of immersion to ripperdoc visits.

Instead of jumping straight to the cyberware menu upon talking to a ripper, V will actually sit down in the clinic's chair before undergoing surgery.

The Dogtown mod does the same for rippers in the Dogtown region of the map, while the Vic-specific mod uses Vic's existing animations from early in the game.

These are mods that, when used in conjunction with other immersion-focused mods, add up to a more detailed experience.

Another two mods that bring just a little more immersion to your time in Night City.

They let you sit down at the game's various bars and actually take a fully-animated drink. You can even select the kind of drink that you want from a dialogue menu.

What's more, the drinks give the same kind of temporary stat buffs that you get from consuming drinks in your inventory. A quick pre-gig bar crawl never hurt anyone!

Just like the Immersive Bartenders mods, this one lets you grab a fully-animated snack or drink from the numerous food vendors found across Night City.

Stat buffs are applied as if you were using items from your inventory, so it actually makes food stalls worth visiting if you're gearing up for some action.

This mod improves the readability of shards, which can be difficult to properly parse — especially if you're in a rush.

Basically, Readable Shards adjusts the text's formatting, making it slightly bigger and adding coloured names to the people who actually wrote the conversations in the first place.

This is a small mod but it can be a surprisingly big difference, particularly if you're a sucker for reading every bit of lore that you find.

A great little mod that adds a security camera system to NCARTS (metros).

By pressing left and right on the d-pad, you can switch to the cameras while you're riding the train, allowing you to view four new perspectives: two cameras shows the length of the carriage that you're on from either end, while the other two shows the outside of the metro from the front and back.

If you want to see more of Night City during your NCART travels, then this mod's an easy recommendation.

If you're absolutely sick of El Capitan giving you unreasonable time limits during his dynamic car-jacking gigs, then this mod's for you.

It simply increases said time limits by 25%, which usually equates to much easier missions. It also means that you can better enjoy the more combat-focused gigs without having to race ahead.

What are your favourite Cyberpunk 2077 mods on PS5? Hand out some recommendations in the comments section below.

Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A former Mass Effect lead has said that Clair Obscur is a good example of what a team could do with a lower budget Mass Effect 5.

Last week BioWare co-founder Trent Oster said that saving Mass Effect 5 – after EA abruptly closed the beloved RPG studio last month – would cost over $200 million to happen due in part to fan expectations of a premium AAA experience, with him noting this would also factor into having "a bigger plan in place for the IP."

Christina Norman – who was the lead cinematics programmer on Mass Effect and lead gameplay and systems designer on Mass Effect 2 and 3 during her tenure at Bioware – reacted to this in a Tweet by sharing a report about Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. The article in question was about the game's budget being under $10 million, with the record-breaking RPG being able to deliver scale and visual fidelity on a budget that is way below a lot of AAA games these days.

You can always spend more but clever small teams can get it done.November 8, 2026

Norman adds "This is a good example of why I think another mass effect game could be made for well under 200 million." She adds, "I mean 5x the budget of Claire Obscure[sic] Expedition 33 should be more than enough." And while you have games like Marvel's Wolverine with a rumored budget of up to $300 million which didn't necessarily land with players, Clair Obscur proves, in Norman's words: "You can always spend more but clever small teams can get it done."

Unfortunately, as anyone who is a fan of Command and Conquer, American McGee's Alice, Burnout, Dungeon Keeper, Dead Space, SSX, Wing Commander, Sim City, Syndicate, Ultima, and a number of other franchises that help me inflate my wordcount will tell you, EA likes to hang onto its IP. So unfortunately, the idea of a new Mass Effect developed independently of EA seems low, no matter the budget.

Canadian politician tears into EA and calls for federal support of BioWare: "These publishers buy developers, run them into the ground, and rip them apart for profit."

#4015. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

#4014. At Dead of Night sequel The Great Hugo is coming "(very) soon"

Baggy Cat Games, the team behind viral FMV horror game At Dead Of Night, has confirmed that a sequel is "coming (very) soon".

At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo picks up where the original game left off and reunites us with Maya as she heads off to investigate a large Tudor manor house.

At Dead Of Night became famous quickly during the pandemic thanks to streamers and content creators like Markiplier, 8-BitRyan, John Wolfe, and DomPlays, who introduced us to Jimmy Hall, a creepy hotel landlord hellbent on recruiting an audience for his late-night comedy show and psychopathic comedy alter ego, Hugo Punch.

The new game, subtitled The Great Hugo, picks up half a decade later.

"Five years later, Maya is still haunted by her experiences in Sea View Hotel," the blurb teases. "Desperate for answers she remembers the ghost box she used in the hotel, left there when she escaped.

"After searching on [auction] sites and in antique shops, she finds a similar looking device, but can’t get it to work. She contacts an old friend and counsellor, Quinn, who had helped her understand her supernatural experiences in the hotel. Quinn recognises the device and knows where they were made - by an inventor who used to live in a large Tudor manor house not far from Sea View - but warns her against trying to get it working. However, Maya ignores his advice and goes on her own investigation."

Quite how long "(very) soon" is, we don't yet know, but we'll keep you posted.

If you're still in the Halloween mood - and why wouldn't you be; horror games are for life, not just for Halloween - the developer of horror hit The Mortuary Assistant released Playable Archive this week as a Halloween freebie.

"Not since the infamous debut of Daikatana has the release of a single game generated so much incensed indignation from early buyers." Our review of Pool of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor didn't hold back. The 2001 dungeon crawler contained, our review said, "A multitude of outrageous bugs," including ones that corrupted saves, made quest items disappear, and most infamously deleted system files when you uninstalled the game.

SNEG's rerelease, available now on Steam and GOG, doesn't have those issues. It adds widescreen, controller support, adjustable combat speed, tooltips, an action bar, and sharpened visuals. If, like me, you skipped this one back in the day because of its reputation for being a hassle to play—even with the eventual patches and community fixes—now it's smooth and problem-free. I've played the opening hours without a single key item vanishing or save file going corrupt.

Don't get the wrong idea, though. Ruins of Myth Drannor isn't Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines. This isn't an RPG masterpiece held back by its buggy release. It's a simplistic turn-based dungeon crawl that's mostly notable for being a spiritual successor to the first Gold Box D&D game, Pool of Radiance, and for adapting the then-new third edition of D&D's rules.

The 3.0 rules were a huge step forward at the time. Any character could choose any class, and Armor Class went up instead of down—you can't imagine how much of a drag it was explaining to new players that lower AC was better than high AC, and ideally you wanted a negative number. It also formalized the central mechanic of rolling a d20 and adding a number to beat a difficulty score. If you've played 5th edition, you'll recognize a lot of its DNA here.

Which is why it's a shame Ruins of Myth Drannor isn't a complete adaptation of those rules. You can't play a wizard—sorcerer is the only option for arcane casters—or a halfling or a gnome. You choose which class to improve when you advance a level, but don't get to decide where your skill points go or what feats to take. A couple of years later, The Temple of Elemental Evil would adapt the 3.5 rules update much more fully. Ruins of Myth Drannor feels rudimentary by comparison.

It's also not much of a story. Set 10 years after the events of Pool of Radiance, a new magical pool has opened in the ruined elven city of Myth Drannor so the evil sorceress and dracolich on the box art can get up to some shenanigans, and Elminster has sent a party of adventurers in to stop them. There's one fun twist to this otherwise bog-standard plot, and it's that you're not that first party of adventurers. You're the B-team sent as backup, but a magic portal mishap means you arrive too late to save the A-team and have to take on their quest.

Which explains why four level-one nobodies now have to clear out hundreds of orcs and skeletons from samey dungeon rooms. It's a slow-paced slog, especially in Myth Drannor's main halls, earning a drip-feed of experience points and gold coins from zombies and ghouls, hoping an orc doesn't score a crit and drop one of your party members in a single blow.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

There are plenty of reasons not to like Ruins of Myth Drannor, but I've been enjoying it in spite of them. It's an undemanding RPG that offers simple pleasures. I get ambushed by skeletons, then realize my cleric is perfectly positioned to hit them all with Turn Undead. I meet a weird slug monster, try talking to him and find out he's friendly. I block doors to protect my sorcerer, while rushing enemy spellcasters before they get their big area-of-effect blast off.

It's junk food D&D, but then I mostly play D&D at a table covered in pizza and beer anyway. Between more demanding games, this is an ideal low-stakes guilty pleasure and I'm glad it's finally back.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Big Issue, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation, published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame.

#4012. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

#4011. Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, selling over 4 million copies in three days

Phantom Blade Zero studio S-Game has announced that its debut title has sold more than 4m copies in its first 72 hours on sale. The game's official X account broke the news alongside a celebratory message, though without providing a per-platform breakdown of copies sold.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" the developer wrote on X.

Phantom Blade Zero is available on Steam and PlayStation 5, but the 4m figure also includes sales made on the China-exclusive Tencent WeGame PC launcher. Prior to launch, Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold over 1m copies before it had even released.

It was always clear the third-person character action game was going to be a hit, we just had to wait for actual figures to be released.

Phantom Blade Zero attracted over 431,000 concurrent players on Steam at launch, a figure that kept risking and rising into the weekend, ultimately settling at a massive 833,921 peak concurrent (via SteamDB). Just in case it wasn't already clear, this is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, beating the likes of Forza Horizon 6 and far outpacing all other major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Ace Combat 8.

Despite the very strong opening weekend's numbers, Phantom Blade Zero has not been able to match or exceed the performance of Black Myth: Wukong, 2024's also-Chinese developed triple-A action game, just yet. The breakout hit, estimated to have sold 30m copies since, is one of Steam's largest debuts ever, peaking at 2,415,714 concurrent players at launch.

In Eurogamer's Phantom Blade Zero review, Emma Kent spoke highly of much of the game, but was critical of its underwhelming narrative and lack of consistency, writing: "This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword."

#4010. GTA 6 Won't Have Any Last Minute Delays, as It's Officially Gone Gold

In case there was any doubt remaining, GTA 6 will definitely be making its debut on 19th November, 2026, with no risk of another delay of some kind.

That's because it's finally been confirmed the game has gone gold, which essentially means the open world action title is ready for release.

This comes via Take-Two's most recent earnings call, during which CEO Strauss Zelnick assured shareholders that GTA 6 had gone gold.

Separately, in an interview with IGN, he also says there are to be no further delays to the release. While that was unlikely given how close we are to the game's arrival, it's never a complete certainty until the software's actually out, so it's nice to have confirmation.

GTA 6 has been in the works for a very long time — at least the eight years since the launch of Red Dead Redemption 2 — so to hear the game is ready to roll out will be an exciting milestone for fans.

I've no doubt there will be additional patches and updates to install as Rockstar further irons out bugs and such.

For those who have pre-ordered the game on PS Store, you can begin pre-loading it starting today, and given the enormous file size, I'd recommend getting that download started as soon as you can.

"Pawn Chess" is whatever you want it to be in Rulehouse.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I have never been particularly good at The Game of Kings, but I do love when an indie developer turns their talents to turning chess into something more funky. Shotgun King stole my heart a few years ago, and now Rulehouse is looking to offer its own spin on the classic.

Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Ted, and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager.

In a generous demo covering the first act of the game, Rulehouse presents a Wario Ware spin on things⁠—in multiple ways. Each level introduces at least one new mechanic or modifier you have to keep track of, starting with the basic "pawns only, first one to the other side of the board wins," and ramping up to a simulated prison break where guards are firing on your pieces, and you have to get your king⁠—here the game's protagonist in a prison jumpsuit⁠—to the exit.

The escalation in complexity had me genuinely scratching my head, stumped at how to proceed at a few points. Rulehouse eschews trad chess pieces as much as possible, only introducing bishops and kings by the very end of the demo⁠—and stubbornly insisting on calling knights "cows" along the way.

Instead, you get stuff like "ice pawns" that shatter on taking an opponent's piece, or "poison pawns" that bring down the opponent's piece with them when they're captured. I'm also quite fond of the upside-down pawns that move on a diagonal, and capture pieces directly in front of them.

Not every new piece is represented on each subsequent level, but it feels like Rulehouse is building a library of modifiers and complications to draw from in the final game, like how the enemy variety in a classic-style FPS campaign ramps up as you go on. It impressed me that Rulehouse could tease such novel puzzles out of one of the most studied and "solved" games to ever exist, and if it can sustain this pace of surprise and delight across a full game, I think it will prove a worthwhile puzzler.

The biggest surprise of all, though, was its presentation and sense of humor. You need something special and specific to stand out with retro pixel art these days, and Rulehouse nails the sound, look, and vibe of the Game Boy Advance. It's got the vibrant, saturated colors I associate with that special little handheld, and all the UI elements are just a little too big, like they're meant to appear on a much lower-resolution screen.

One of my favorite flourishes is how Rulehouse pairs very crisp and clean bits of pixel art with super bitcrushed and noisy backgrounds, often sourced from real photography. It's a technique that was frequently deployed on the GBA, and in addition to pure nostalgia "hey, remember this?" appeal, it adds a uniquely early aughts surreality to the proceedings, the kind I associate with stuff like Wario Ware or, less intentionally, all those really boo-boo, memory-holed movie tie-ins and ill-advised home console ports to the GBA.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The music, similarly, nails a specific sensibility, a kind of synthy funk I associate with Wario Ware, Earthbound or, more recently, Balatro. Rulehouse is a love letter to the Game Boy Advance from people who thoroughly, obsessively, get the console.

Rulehouse is also genuinely funny. Its narrative bits have a strong rate of Smiles Per Minute™, and that dovetails nicely with the surprise rule changes and offbeat art⁠ to result in something that's just kinda nice⁠. Rulehouse is aiming to launch some time in 2027, and for now, you can wishlist it or check out the demo for yourself on Steam.

#4008. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

#4007. Soulframe to launch into free open alpha this week, as Warframe devs go head-to-head with WoW: Forever

Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of an alpha) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.

The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

As you do so, new resources will be obtainable and side activities like fishing will be unlocked. You'll also be able to train up a small wolf pet into a full-on mount in the process. Previously, players were just thrust into the open world to explore and figure things out as they go, so this should provide something of an introduction to the game's open map. It won't be totally finished when released mind you, with updates to the Veillands system coming in the future.

On top of that, there's a new Pact called the Ode Shrike coming with the update. It's a tricksy trapper with spikes, balloon snares, bombs and chains to disrupt enemies as you whittle them down.

Could this be enough to win people over to Digital Extreme's newest project? Time will tell - but in the meantime its long-lasting sci-fi MMO Warframe is taking players to the Tau system in a major next step in the game's narrative this December. It comes with a detective noir inspired main quest, playable warframe, and even an in-universe Poker equivalent.

Ahead of Ocarina of Time, Mario 64 was a learning moment for Miyamoto

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo has dropped another banger. The Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time Remake has arrived to fanfare almost matching the release of the 1998 original. But according to Shigeru Miyamoto, around the time that Link was coming face to face with the Great Deku Tree, Nintendo had been struggling to perfect the balance between innovation and execution.

Speaking to Keni Eno in 1996 (via Shmupulations), shortly after the release of Mario 64 and a couple of years before Ocarina of Time, Miyamoto was asked about the rising complexity and polish of Nintendo games, and whether he thought they should offer a sense of escapism. In response, he suggested that the fact Mario and Zelda games were being planned out at the same time meant that the "boundary" between the two franchises had "started to disappear."

Eno's comments focused heavily on the changes between pre-release and retail versions of Mario 64, but Miyamoto's answer was that while early demos might have felt a little more innovative, the polish of the retail version was better. However, "if you ask whether Nintendo should be satisfied as long as the commercial polish is high, I don't think so," he said. "There are two kinds of games - well-made games and interesting games - and the public perception of Nintendo's games has gradually shifted from 'interesting' to 'well-made'. We've ended up pouring a lot of our energy into that side of things."

Miyamoto said that with Mario 64 in the rear-view, Nintendo had "proven we can make a solid 3D action game. Because of that, I think we can aim for something more interesting next time."

It's not immediately clear what that 'next time' was supposed to be, but Nintendo's next big 3D action game would prove to be Ocarina of Time - a title that would prove to push the envelope in terms of both ambition and execution, securing all-timer status and a MetaCritic score of 99 that is unlikely to ever be meaningfully challenged. It would prove to be a highlight in an already-legendary run for Nintendo: Mario Kart 64 and Star Fox 64 launched in 1997, and Banjo-Kazooie, Pokemon Red/Blue, and F-Zero X would launch ahead of Ocarina in 1998, with Mario Party and Super Smash Bros following up in 1999.

But while the original launch of Ocarina of Time makes that balance between ambition and execution clear, the remake muddies the waters. While it's clear that Nintendo has done very well in delivering on its mission to recreate the game, can a remake ever capture the innovation of the original? And while the Switch 2 has given us the likes of Donkey Kong Bananza and Pokopia, it's also slipped a little with the more muted receptions around games like Mario Kart World and Pokemon Legends Z-A.

It's probably impossible to stay on the kind of winning run that Nintendo found itself in during the late 90s, but Miyamoto's assertion - that studios should strive to create games that are both ambitiously innovative and technically excellent - is something that I don't feel like I always see from the company in the mid-2020s. Ocarina of Time might remain a legendary release, but its remake is a reminder of just how much the industry has changed in the last three decades.

#4005. Persona 4 Revival Wasn't Meant to Be Part of Packed February 2027 Release Schedule

Persona 4 Revival was initially designed to launch for PS5 in the late summer months of this year, not the very crowded February 2027 release calendar it's now found itself in.

In an interview with 3DMGAME, chief producer Kazuhisa Wada shared the original plan was to launch the remake "as early as possible — we originally planned to release it about six months earlier, which would have been just in time for summer, but we ultimately couldn't make it that way".

The original Persona 4 often sparks memories of summer for players, as a large part of the game takes place during the season and includes trips to the beach and festivals specific to that part of the year. Putting the PS5 remake out during that same season would have made a lot of sense, but the Atlus executive claims the firm "couldn't make it that way".

It's not clear whether Wada is referring to development issues or a different problem that affected the release.

Either way, Persona 4 Revival now launches on 18th February 2027, a month full of other big PS5 releases. The delay to God of War Laufey gives everything else a touch more breathing room, but the schedule still looks like this:

As an RPG, its strongest competition is probably Fable, which releases just five days after Persona 4 Revival. The Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis remake should take up a lot of mindshare in the weeks before it, too.

We shall still play it in February, but getting to experience it again during those quieter summer months would have been bliss.

Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.

Yikes, three remakes in one month. I'll only be getting Atelier, thanks.

I'm looking forward to this, but I'm worried about the voice acting.

Persona 3's voice acting on PS2 was ok, but Persona 4 was revolutionary in how good its dubbing was. It was the first anime styled game that I know of that had truely amazing voice acting.

I have preorder the Tomb Raider remake and I will most likely get Atelier since I am a fan of the series but to be fair I have no interest in Persona at all. I find the silent protagonist an extremely outdated concept. And in Persona 4 I did not like that the antagonist was evil for the sake of being evil. It is not easy to get this concept right.

@belmont I respectfully disagree. Silent protagonists are fine still in my opinion, when they're meant to represent you, the player. It isn't Yu who's romancing all the girls in the game it's.....you (only noticed that was a pun). And the antagonist's motives actually do tie in well to the game's overall themes of finding the truth.

Muramasa, Persona 4 Revival, and Romancing Saga 3 for me.

#4004. Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.

#4003. "We're doing great," says id Software boss, despite losing "about half of our studio" amid devastating Xbox cuts

Iconic Doom and Quake developer id Software was among the most heavily impacted Microsoft-owned studios during Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating business "reset" earlier this year, with around 136 employees reportedly losing their jobs.

In the wake of those layoffs, id Software co-studio director Marty Stratton was recently asked about the current state of the developer, and how it has been affected by Sharma's cuts. "We're doing great," Stratton told journalists at a recent event (via IGN).

"Not to handwave the [layoffs] away… everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that," he continued. "But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department."

This is not the first time a senior id Software member has pushed back on the narrative the studio has been "nerfed into the ground and gutted". Hugo Martin, id's other co-studio head previously claimed the remaining team is "the size we were when we made Doom 2016, and id Tech is very much alive and well".

Sharma's Xbox reset will ultimately see 3,200 jobs cut across Microsoft's gaming division, with many of those still to come. Those impacted by the first wave of cuts in July, however, included developers working on the id Software's id Tech engine. This is the engine behind all of the studio's games, and is known to be among the most performant engines, consistently producing visually-impressive games that require modest specs to run.

Following the layoffs, many inside and outside the studio said the id Tech team had been gutted. Longtime id Software programmer Chris Hays, who notably wasn't among those let go, said at the time, "It is hard to make a game that is triple-A, that is like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard I mean impossible". Hays also claimed "entire departments" and "entire disciplines" are gone.

While Stratton hasn't addressed those comments directly, he revealed id Software is now "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the modern Wolfenstein games, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. "We've always had a very close partnership with [MachineGames], but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]," he explained.

"We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead."

Id Software's next project remains unclear. MachineGames, on the other hand, recently said it's not done with Wolfenstein, so it's possible a sequel to 2017's The New Colossus is in the works.

Deadline reports that a Canadian documentary about the history of BioWare was already two years into filming when EA closed the studio. Now, it's becoming a sad goodbye to a legendary developer.

"The BioWare founders are my hometown heroes," the documentary's writer and director Akash Sherman said. "It's a privilege and responsibility to share the journey of underdogs who came together to create deeply beloved storytelling. Their golden era kindled a spark in me and in an entire generation. With the studio's recent closure, the film is now a profound valediction."

The documentary, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, features interviews with the studio's founders, Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk, and Augustine Yip, as well as developers Casey Hudson, Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen, and Caroline Livingstone, voice actor Jennifer Hale, former CEO of EA John Riccitello, and vice president of Lucasfilm Games Douglas Reilly.

"When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and genuinely moved," Muzyka and Zeschuk said in a statement. "BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about deeply emotionally engaging stories and characters, brought to life by the amazingly talented people on our dev teams, and our excellent production and distribution partners who helped us bring those stories successfully to all corners of the planet, and our passionate fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We're proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again."

Massive Effect: The BioWare Story is scheduled for release next year. Meanwhile, composer Sam Hulick has shared a re-scored version of the leaked trailer for Mass Effect Universe as his own way of saying goodbye, though apparently Amazon's Mass Effect TV series is still in the works.

#4001. The Legend of Khiimori's Mongolian Expanse update brings in frosty mountains and scorching deserts that'll require a lot more than a fur coat and a sturdy horse

Another day, another opportunity for some horsing around! I'm being literal here, to be clear, as a new update for The Legend of Khiimori dropped yesterday. It's called The Mongolian Expanse, opening up the map a whole lot more and making a sweep of other additions to the game.

Previously, you might have looked out unto the snowy mountainscapes and the scorching deserts and thought "boy howdy am I glad I can't go there, those temperatures look like a nightmare to deal with!" Well, good news, as you now can head to those locales, each with "their own waystations, Yam nodes, named places, chests and bandit caches."

You don't want to wander there without some amount of prep, however, as the mountains are cold and difficult to climb, with wolves none too kind to humans like you. The desert, of course, is really hot, for both you and your horse. Both additions remind me of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and its use of extreme temperatures acting as a sort of challenge gate. Neat stuff!

The buck doesn't stop there with this update though. You'll find a whole host of new wildlife, ranging from wild boars, to gobi bears and camels. Of course, a horse game wouldn't be one without more horse, which there is! It's a new breed called the Marwari, a horse that is "built for endurance and especially resistant to heat, a strong partner for long, punishing Desert crossings." Beyond that, you'll also find more than 60 new horse skills, all findable across specific regions and for specific breeds.

It's a nice beefy update with plenty more tweaks, additions and fixes on top of everything mentioned above. When it comes to the mountains and desert, you can also expect some big additions there, as this is only the first part of this update. You can read about everything else the update offers right here on Steam.

#4000. Over a decade later, Bloodborne remains so popular it reportedly sold a quarter of a million copies this year alone

Bloodborne, FromSoftware's singular Lovecraftian action-RPG, has reportedly sold more than 251,000 copies this year alone.

That's according to Alinea Analytics head of market analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed the figure in a post on X, noting this brings Bloodborne's total sales up to an estimated 10.4m copies, generating $317m (around £236m) in revenue. Elliot also claimed more than half a million people played Bloodborne in October through PlayStation Plus.

Additionally, 12 percent of those are said to have played Elden Ring during the month, while 6 percent played Dark Souls 3, and 5 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. There's a cohort of gamers who are always bouncing between different From[Software] games," Elliott pointed out. "Can't blame them, especially with this one."

Bloodborne is a PlayStation exclusive that sadly never left the PS4, despite consistent calls from fans for ports and remasters. While the game is playable on PS5 through backwards compatibility, Bloodborne barely benefits from the console's advanced hardware, only seeing smoother frame pacing. In other words, it's the same game with barely any perceptible upgrades.

Before Sony closed down Demon's Souls remake developer Bluepoint Games earlier this year, the studio reportedly pitched a Bloodborne remake, but original developer FromSoftware didn't want it to happen. When news of the pitch came to light, former Sony Interactive Entertainment Shuhei Yoshida said Bloodborne has a special place in director Hidetaka Miyazaki's heart and speculated the reason it hasn't had a remake is because Miyazaki would prefer to do it himself but doesn't have the time.

"Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created," Yoshida said at the time. "So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

James Gunn says "the characters we set up will live on" as he departs as the co-CEO of DC Studios

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

James Gunn has released a separate, lengthy statement amid the news that he and co-CEO Peter Safran are no longer the heads of DC Studios.

"There have been so many highs along the way: releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs., the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments," Gunn wrote on his personal Instagram account.

Gunn also lamented that he "disliked the at-times corporate nature of the job" and had the "most difficulty" with "dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

"So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I'm also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That's not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we've just been engaged on another DC project which I'm writing, and we'll see where it goes after that. And of course, the characters we set up will live on." You can read the full statement below.

The statement comes amid the shocking news that Gunn and Safran would be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham, effective December 1. The duo was first appointed to the position back in 2022, having released three movies: Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface, and four TV shows: Creature Commandos, Peacemaker season 2, The Penguin, and Lanterns, over the last four years. Still to come are Man of Tomorrow, The People V Gorilla Grodd, Creature Commandos season 2, and the long-awaited The Batman: Part II.

Of course, this change is no doubt part of the Skydance merger, which sees Paramount in full control of Warner Bros. and everything Warner Bros. owns. It's worth noting that, before Gunn and Safran were appointed, Warner Bros. executives reportedly wanted an overhaul of DC in favor of putting classic heroes back at the forefront and making them a bit less dark/more kid-friendly. That said, it's possible that Skydance executives want fewer projects like The People v. Gorilla Grodd and Creature Commandos, and more big-hitters on screen, like Wonder Woman or Aquaman... and finally Batman (who still only exists as part of Matt Reeves' Elseworlds; the DCU has yet to cast a Batman). It also probably doesn't help that Supergirl was a massive critical and commercial failure.

Man of Tomorrow hits theaters on July 9, 2027. For more, here are all the upcoming DC movies and shows announced before Gunn's departure.

#3997. After a 16-year long dev period, Faraway, a shooting star arcade game about siphoning the energy of other stars, is out now

Lord almighty, video games take a while to make, 'ey? Especially if you're just one person working on it by yourself. Such is the case with Faraway, out today, an arcade game that reminds me of the early days of PS3 indies "about a shooting star that creates constellations to stay alive," all made single-handedly by creator of cult-classic mobile game Eliss, Steph Thirion. Did I mention that Faraway took 16 years to make? Like I said, game development is a lengthy process.

Looking at Faraway, and knowing how long it took to produce, it doesn't surprise me to come from a dev who managed to release a mobile game in the early days of the platform, long before free-to-play got its chokehold on the industry. It also really does feel like it should be sitting amongst the likes of PixelJunk, this thing should be something I'm desperate to play on my PS3 while I wait for my controller to charge.

As mentioned, you are a shooting star, a "spark meant to shine and vanish in a blink." But still you persist, connecting to and wrapping yourself around starts to "harvest their energy," in turn lengthening your own life, and of course, in arcadey fashion, racking up a nice score. It looks like game design as poetry, everything you're looking at procedurally generated to bring freshness to every run. I can fully envision this as a "one more run" kind of arcade game, the best kind, especially in an age long past the need to shove in another of your hard earned coins.

Faraway conceptually charms me because it taps into a style of game we don't get to see much of any more. What I'm saying is, I'm just a teensy bit sick of how many roguelikes there are, but that doesn't mean I don't want a game I can just hop in and out of at my own whims. Sure, arcade games might not be in vogue, I just miss them a bit. In any case, Faraway is available to pick up on Steam right now. Seems like it'll be worth a punt!

#3996. As the controversy around AI-created video game copies continues, Anthropic seemingly restricts Claude's cloning abilities

An update to Anthropic's Claude AI software has seemingly blocked the creation of outright clones or copies of existing games. Instead, Claude has been altered to only create "original" games.

Among the first to share news of the change was X user Chasm, who posted a screenshot showing the new rule, purportedly added around 27th October. "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets," it reads. "Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”.

While Anthropic is yet to issue an official statement on the new rule, technical staff member Addy Osmani commented beneath Chasm's post, confirming the change's legitimacy. He noted it was included because "using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy", but added that creating original games and those built with a user's own assets should still be possible.

Following the new rule's inclusion, users on GitHub shared newfound barriers they'd run into as a result. Reports included being blocked from creating digital modules for board games, and from recreating a commercially produced board game for personal use. Eurogamer has contacted Anthropic for comment on the rule change and its stance on AI game copies.

The modifications to Claude have appeared at a time when AI copies of games have drawn increasing ire, with game communities pushing back against them and developers pulling public-facing demos in fear of having their work stolen. AI-assisted copies of triple-A games have also emerged, including a version of Mario Kart 8 playable in an internet browser. However, this was taken down in a matter of days, presumably thanks to a legal notice from Nintendo.

Of course, even if Claude is prevented from making game copies, other AI tools, such as Deepseek, still lack similar restrictions. Until such measures are ubiquitous, the issue will continue. Given Claude's position as one of the most popular commercial AI tools out there, however, this will certainly make a dent in the problem.

I've been playing Path of Exile for almost ten years and have put a ton of hours into PoE2 since it entered early access, and in all that time there's one feature that I've wished for more than any other. More than stash tabs, more than fancy microtransactions, even more than finally finding a mirror in the wild.

What I want more than anything is a death recap: a way to finally have some idea why my turbo powerful character that's blasting through a map went pop. At an interview at ExileCon this weekend, game director Jonathan Rogers confirmed that it's finally coming to Path of Exile 2.

I don't know whether Grinding Gear intended to announce the feature this weekend, but during the keynote's live demo of new content, Mark Roberts' character died. And there before our eyes, live and in person, was a death recap screen. After we all got done cheering, Rogers laughed and confirmed that the feature was present and would be included in the full 1.0 release coming up on December 11.

"I was really worried that it wasn't going to be useful enough or accurate enough, but we got it to a place that I'm fairly happy with," Rogers said when I asked him to confirm that the feature would be present at launch.

"The thing that's not quite good is the damage over time tracking," he added. "We do tell you that you took it but we don't know where it came from.”

Thankfully, it's a bit easier to parse taking damage over time in the game already, and he assured us that they're working on getting that sorted out as well.

One of the reasons that the death recap is such an important feature is that it can be incredibly hard to parse exactly what you should be focusing on with your character once you get to the endgame. A lot of times you've maxed your resistances, have a decent life pool, and a good amount of either armour, evasion, or energy shield, but still something comes along and explodes you. And since there are often many monsters on the screen, to say nothing of all the explosions or arrows or minions or ice comets that you yourself are spamming, it can be almost impossible to figure out what happened.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"The most important thing to be was like… here's the damage you took and how much of it was mitigated," says Rogers. "My goal was to drive you toward 'what is the thing I need to fix about my character to have avoided this.'" A big physical hit? Maybe some more evasion or life. Cold damage? Maybe grab a couple jewels with + to max cold res.

Sometimes though, the problem isn't with you. Sometimes you get a killer crab that kills hundreds of thousands of players due to a typo. He thinks the death recap will help here, too.

"This may sound a bit funny, but I think it'll actually give our players an avenue to complain about the correct things. Sometimes we just have monsters that have wrong balance values, it happens, and in the heat of battle you don't know what it was. Now you'll be able to say this particular monster is the one that has the damage that's off the hook and then it allows them to direct us to that."

Despite having their own internal systems to monitor monster behavior, nothing beats the urgency and immediacy of a legion of players crying out at once on the internet about killer crabs.

Mark Roberts went on to say that he anticipates that the feature "will 100% be asked for en masse" by Path of Exile 1 players, and if it is, they'll port that functionality over as soon as they can.

As for me, the death recap is but one of many amazing features I'm looking forward to in Path of Exile 2's full release. It will be available on December 11th.

Russ has been playing PC games since the top of the line graphics were in ASCII and has been obsessed with them just about as long. When he's not writing about videogames, he's teaching karate, cooking an overly complicated dish, or attempting to raise his daughter with a well rounded classical education (Civilization, Doom, and Baldur's Gate, of course). He's probably mapping in Path of Exile right now.

#3994. Ablahshikar is a maximalist, sickos only salvage-survival CRPG about ripping organs out of warships and pawning off strange goods that's now out in early access

I don't know what's going on, and I like it

Sometimes, you come across a game and instantly know it's for the sickos. Today that is Ablahshikar, a "turn-based salvage-survival CRPG adrift on the Candle Sea" where you rip out the organs of enemy warships to "rebuild your vessel into a doomed chimera," that is out now in early access. To be honest I could have just called it a CRPG and still labelled it as a game for sickos, yet everything that's going on here is obviously just doubling down on the sick factor.

Ablahshikar is a particular flavour of maximalism. Having not played it, it feels a bit impossible describe, I mean, just have a read of some of the game's Steam page: "Lo, destiny crooks a finger only to those whose eyes peer beyond þe next tempest. Take custody of a faltering war-barge that wanders the outer brine of Dastgerd. Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." I don't know what any of that means! And I love it. Reminds me of Hylics in that the game's world is not translating itself for its audience; you take what you're given, and you figure it out yourself.

Judging from trailers and screenshots, there's a mix of activities to be getting on with. Occasionally you'll be piloting a strange, not alien, but definitely ancient ship of some kind in an arcadey sort of fashion. Then occasionally there's something that resembles Caves of Qud, i.e. some odd, 2D maybe dungeon crawling where your moves are dictated by individual keys on your keyboard. Then there's Disco Elysiumy cutscenes that feel like a video game designed in the year 1200 by someone from the year 2200, aesthetically anyway. As I said, it is a particular flavour of maximalism.

Truthfully, I do not know if I am sicko enough for Ablahshikar. Its mighty vision is terrifying, but I certainly am curious about it. Right now it's less than a fiver, and it'll only be in early access for roughly a couple of months where the price will then go up, so perhaps it's best to get in at the ground floor. If you are one such sicko, then you can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3993. One World of Warcraft: Forever player is working on a first-person mod that's a love letter to retro RPGs like Hexen and Morrowind

One World of Warcraft: Forever player is attempting to turn Blizzard's new MMO endeavour into a Morrowind-esque first-person fantasy RPG, full of retro animations harkening back to the good ol' days. And there's no generative AI in sight.

The project, known as Retro Forever, is the work of modder Arhkain, who's so far published two dev vlogs detailing the nature of his work. He opens the first vlog by describing how he always wanted to view the world of Azeroth through his character's eyes, but was met with a lack of adequate options to support this style of play. That encouraged him to find his own solutions, which is how Retro Forever was born.

The result is a WoW Forever mod aiming to incorporate "fully immersive" first-person graphics - whether it be for combat, cooking, or flying across the world - with a presentation style reminiscent of classic first-person fantasy games like Morrowind or Hexen. In fact, the mod currently uses assets pulled and modified from those games.

Retro Forever - which is described as a "clever combination of addons that already exist" - includes a custom user interface, as well as animations attached to specific spells and abilities. That means, if you're a mage and attack an enemy with a spell, you'll see a custom animation of your character doing that spell.

The bad news is the mod isn't publicly available right now, and currently only works with a selection of mage spells and other class abilities. However, that's set to expand - and Arhkain recently revealed an artist has expressed interest in joining the project for original asset creation.

As for the no-generative AI deal, Arhkain said the tool "wouldn't help" in the mod's development. And when Retro Forever has been updated with original art to replace its currently borrowed assets, it should also dodge any legal pitfalls too. Nice!

With World of Warcraft: Forever set to release this Wednesday, 4th November, excitement is abound for the new spin on an old MMO. Judging from my time with the beta, the game is looking rather good!
